draft.title: Tests for congruent triangles
card: all three pairs of matching sides are equal.
two pairs of sides are equal, and the angles between those sides (the included angles) are equal.
two pairs of angles are equal, and a pair of matching sides is equal. The side can be anywhere, as long as it matches.
both triangles have a right angle, the hypotenuses are equal, and one other pair of sides is equal.
draft.remember: Meeting one of SSS, SAS, AAS or RHS proves congruence. Two sides and a non-included angle does not.

a.q: Triangles ABC and DEF have \(AB = DE\), \(BC = EF\) and \(\angle B = \angle E\). Which test shows they are congruent?
a.why: The equal angle B lies between sides AB and BC, and angle E lies between DE and EF. So it is two sides and the included angle, which is SAS. It is not SSS, because only two pairs of sides are known to be equal.
a.clue: Where does the equal angle sit compared with the two equal sides?

b.q: In triangles PQR and XYZ, \(PQ = XY = 7\) cm and \(QR = YZ = 5\) cm. Also \(\angle P = \angle X = 40^{\circ}\). What can Mia say?
opts: She cannot tell if they are congruent
b.why: Angle P is not between sides PQ and QR, so it is a non-included angle. Two sides and a non-included angle is not enough to prove congruence. SAS is the tempting wrong choice, because it needs the angle between the two sides.
b.clue: Check which two sides meet at angle P.

b.best: She cannot tell if they are congruent

problems.detail: The right option, 'She cannot tell if they are congruent', is the longest and the only one not in the form 'They are congruent by ...'. A student could pick it as the odd one out without knowing the idea.
The card's bullets never explain the two-sides-and-a-non-included-angle case. Only the remember line mentions it, yet question b depends on it. One card line saying why it fails would help.

proposal.title: Tests for congruent triangles
card: SSS: all three pairs of matching sides are equal. SAS: two pairs of sides are equal, and so are the angles between them, called the included angles.
AAS: two pairs of angles are equal, and one pair of matching sides is equal. RHS: both have a right angle, equal hypotenuses and one other pair of equal sides.
Two sides and a non-included angle, an angle not between those sides, is not a test. The same three facts can fit two different triangles, so congruence is not proved.
To choose a test, mark the equal parts. Then check where each equal angle sits compared with the equal sides.
proposal.remember: One of SSS, SAS, AAS or RHS proves congruence. Two sides and a non-included angle does not.

a.q: Triangles ABC and DEF have \(AB = DE\), \(BC = EF\), and angle B equals angle E. Which test shows they are congruent?
a.why: Angle B lies between sides AB and BC, and angle E lies between DE and EF. So it is two sides and the included angle, which is SAS. It is not SSS, because only two pairs of sides are known to be equal.
a.clue: Where does the equal angle sit compared with the two equal sides?

b.q: In triangles PQR and XYZ, \(PQ\) and \(XY\) are both 7 cm, \(QR\) and \(YZ\) are both 5 cm, and angles P and X are both \(40^{\circ}\). What should Mia conclude?
opts: Not proved, as the angle is not between the sides
Congruent by SAS, as two sides and an angle match
Congruent by RHS, as two pairs of sides match
Not proved, as SAS only works with a right angle
b.why: Sides PQ and QR meet at Q, so angle P is not between them. Two sides and a non-included angle can fit two different triangles, so congruence is not proved. SAS is tempting, but it needs the angle between the two equal sides.
b.clue: Check which two sides meet at angle P.

b.best: Not proved, as the angle is not between the sides
